The timeline plots TAI, GPS, Unix and UT1 against UTC from 1972 with a continuous-UTC projection whose cutover date, excess length of day and growth are inputs. The step vs smear tab compares POSIX step, a 24-hour linear smear, UTC-SLS and a monotonic clock around 2016-12-31T23:59:60, and replays a seeded two-host request log that counts reordered lines, receives before sends, backwards clocks and mismeasured round trips. The library bench shows outputs recorded from real runs of Node Date, the Temporal polyfill, CPython and PostgreSQL 16 on ten edge cases (for example, Temporal clamps :60 to :59, and Postgres accepts :60 but rejects :60.5), each with a hand-written note in place of the suggested Claude explainer. Four fix-the-bug exercises (timeout, rate limiter, billing duration, log merge) run hidden tests in a Web Worker against a simulated stepping clock. Limitations: UT1 before the cutover is a schematic sawtooth, not IERS data, and the projection is a two-parameter model. The 2027-05-20 cutover default comes from the idea brief and is unverified (the 2022 CGPM resolution only says by or before 2035). The bench is recorded rather than live. The exercises are JavaScript only, with no Pyodide. 47 vitest tests, 99.7% statement coverage on core.
projects.publicNotes: An interactive lab on leap seconds and the bugs they cause. A timeline plots atomic time, GPS, Unix time and Earth's rotation against everyday UTC since 1972, and lets you project what happens once leap seconds stop. Compare how servers handle the extra second at 23:59:60, by stepping the clock back or by smearing it, and see the reordered logs and backwards clocks that result. A bench shows how common date libraries and a database handle ten edge cases, and four fix-the-bug exercises check your code with hidden tests. Limitation: the library results were recorded from earlier runs, not run live.

projects.notes: Built in one session as a static TypeScript app with no backend and no LLM. One Redis-like console (SET with EX, GET, DEL, EXPIRE, TTL, TICK, RANGE, FILL, CAPACITY, SEED) drives four buildings at once: a separate-chaining hash map that doubles past load 0.75, a CLRS B-tree of minimum degree 2 (split on the way down on insert; borrow or merge on the way down on delete), a skip list with seeded p = 1/2 towers so every student sees the same city, and a 5-slot LRU cache (hash index plus recency list) that forgets on purpose. Each building reports structural events (rehash, collision, split, grow, merge, borrow, shrink, promote, evict), highlights the keys that moved, and keeps a cost meter of probes, comparisons and moves with last, amortized (running mean) and worst-case figures; RANGE shows ordered structures walking forward while the hash map and cache scan everything. TTLs use a logical clock swept on TICK. Five predict-then-reveal guided tours are built in, and instructors edit tour JSON in the page and share it in the URL fragment, replacing the suggested Supabase storage. Keyboard navigation between buildings, a polite live region, and a text narration mode that describes every building in words. Limitations: changes appear as highlights and event notes rather than tweened animation, there is no 3D view, the B-tree degree and initial bucket count are fixed, and the city holds at most 40 keys. 71 vitest tests (including a 600-step randomized B-tree invariant check and a test that every tour answer matches what the city does), 99.8% statement coverage on core.
projects.publicNotes: Turns four data structures into buildings in a city so students can see how each stores the same data. You type simple commands to add, look up, expire or delete keys, and a hash map, a B-tree, a skip list and a small cache all react at once, showing splits, merges, evictions and the cost of each step. Five guided tours ask students to predict what will happen before revealing it, and instructors can write their own tours and share them by link. A text narration mode describes every building in words. Limitation: the city holds at most 40 keys, and changes appear as highlights rather than animation.

projects.notes: Built in one session as a static TypeScript app with no backend and no LLM. Connect Four 7x6 with a fixed network interface: an MLP with 84 inputs (mover's pieces, opponent's pieces), up to three hidden layers (relu or tanh) and 7 linear outputs, playing the legal column with the highest logit, under a 5,000-parameter budget. Submissions are plain JSON weight files validated for shape, finiteness and budget, so the ladder never runs student code. Two in-browser training methods run in a Web Worker: imitation of a house bot (Scripted heuristic, Lookahead-2 or Lookahead-4; every tied-best column as a soft target, mirrored data, Adam on a legal-masked softmax) and a truncation-selection evolution strategy that can fine-tune an imitation net. House bots are Random, a scripted win/block/avoid-blunder heuristic and depth-4 alpha-beta. The round-robin ladder plays fixed two-ply openings with colour swaps and rates bots with an order-independent Bradley-Terry fit on the Elo scale (Random pinned at 1000), plus an efficiency board of Elo above Random per 1k parameters. Milestone badges (90% vs Random, above 50% vs Scripted, ladder rank), a replay viewer with per-ply network probabilities and missed-win/missed-block/played-under-a-win flags, an experiment log that exports a Markdown or CSV ablation table, and a NumPy reference runtime checked against the browser by a 131-position parity fixture. The suggested Flask server, React viewer and Supabase storage are replaced by the browser and localStorage. Limitations: no shared server or accounts (the instructor runs the official ladder by loading every file into one browser), single-threaded JS training, Connect Four only, no built-in self-play. 46 vitest tests, 100% statement coverage on core.
projects.publicNotes: A class competition where students train tiny neural networks to play Connect Four. Each student trains a small network right in the browser, either by imitating a built-in opponent or by evolving it, and submits a plain file of numbers, so no student code ever runs on the ladder. A round-robin ladder rates every bot, also ranks them by strength for their size, and awards milestones, while a replay viewer flags missed wins and blocks move by move. Experiment results export as tables for a lab report. Limitation: there are no accounts or shared server, so the instructor runs the official ladder by loading every file into one browser.

projects.notes: Built in one session as a static TypeScript app with no backend. The {p,q} polygon centred at the origin splits into 2p right triangles with angles π/p, π/q and π/2, and the three mirrors of that triangle generate the tiling. Isometries are stored as SU(1,1) Möbius maps z ↦ (αz + β)/(β̄z + ᾱ), applied to z or z̄, and renormalised after every product. Tiles are generated breadth-first from the tile under the screen centre, up to a depth limit and a minimum on-screen size. Each stroke is folded into the fundamental triangle once and redrawn under every group element (or only the orientation-preserving coset in rotation mode), so freehand doodles become Circle Limit patterns and the geodesic brush draws arcs orthogonal to the rim. Widths are stored in hyperbolic units, so copies thin towards the boundary at the right rate. Dragging applies a pure hyperbolic translation, and after each step the view is swapped for an equivalent one composed with a group element, which keeps precision however far you travel (a test drags about 360 units). Double-clicking glides a point to the centre. A measure tool gives hyperbolic distance and a triangle's angles, angle sum and area. SVG export uses real arcs, and share links pack tiling, symmetry, view and strokes into a compact binary in the URL fragment. Batching shading fills and stroke copies took a {7,3} frame from about 900 ms to 70 ms in headless Chromium. Limitations: Canvas 2D only, with no WebGL path for very deep tilings; one width per stroke, so long strokes do not taper; freehand segments are polylines rather than geodesic pieces; measurement marks are not shared or exported; no pinch-zoom. 58 vitest tests, 100% statement coverage on core.
projects.publicNotes: Draw in the hyperbolic plane and watch your doodle repeat across an endless tiling, like M.C. Escher's Circle Limit prints. Pick a tiling and a symmetry, then paint freehand or with a brush that follows the disk's curved straight lines; every stroke is copied across the whole pattern and thins correctly toward the rim. Drag to travel as far as you like, measure distances and triangle angles, export an SVG, or share your drawing as a link. Limitation: there is no pinch-zoom on touch screens.

projects.notes: Built in one session as a static TypeScript app with no backend and no LLM. Every piece, historical or invented, is one line of a Betza-like notation (atoms, riders, ranges such as B{2,}, a second leg such as the giraffe's F>R{3,}, and m/c/f/b/l/r/s/v/n/j/p/i modifiers) compiled once per variant into rays that the move generator, the highlight overlay and the engine all walk. Play: Timur chess on the 11x10 board with both citadels (a king entering the opponent's citadel draws; stalemate loses), against a negamax alpha-beta engine with iterative deepening and quiescence in a Web Worker, plus simplified classic chess. Piece lab: live animated reach with placeable blockers, a mobility-based value estimate, drop-in replacement in Timur or classic chess, six-game engine-vs-engine balance tests with alternating colours, and share links that encode the spec in the URL. A pieces tab gives each historical piece a history card. Limitations: no king swap, no extra royals (the prince is an ordinary king-mover), the pawn of pawns promotes straight to a prince, citadel ownership is an interpretation, classic chess has no castling or en passant, the Claude English-to-notation step is replaced by examples, and values are a heuristic. 82 vitest tests, 99% statement coverage on core.
projects.publicNotes: Play Tamerlane chess, the medieval Timur variant on an 11 by 10 board with citadels, against a computer opponent, or invent your own pieces. Each piece is described in one short line of movement notation, so you can design a new one, watch where it can reach around blockers, get an estimated value and drop it into Timur or classic chess. Six computer-versus-computer games test whether your piece unbalances the game, and a share link sends it to anyone. History cards explain each historical piece. Limitation: some rules are simplified, such as no king swap, and the classic chess mode has no castling or en passant.

projects.notes: Built in one session as a static TypeScript app with no backend and no LLM; the GPU is simulated, not WebGPU, so every browser gives the same numbers. Students write kernels in a small CUDA-like language (let, if/else, for, while, return, shared arrays, sync(), selects, atomicAdd) and pick the launch; the simulator runs each warp of 32 lanes with an active mask, so divergent branches run both paths, loops run while any lane continues, and warps pause at barriers (a sync() reached by only some lanes is an error). A cost model charges per warp instruction, per 128-byte global segment, per queued shared-memory bank and per serialized atomic, spreads blocks over four SMs, and compares the result with a one-core CPU estimate. Every access is bounds-checked and race-checked (shared memory between barriers, global memory within and across blocks). Twelve levels cover indexing, bounds, block size, divergence, grid-stride loops, coalescing, races and atomics, shared-memory reduction, barrier placement, bank conflicts, tiling and privatized histograms; each run gets stars against a reference solution's par, counters, an SM timeline and a warp inspector with per-lane masks coloured by segment or bank. The suggested Claude hints are replaced by a deterministic diagnosis built from the simulator's counters and traces, pointing at lines; the Supabase dashboard is replaced by JSON progress exports that an instructor loads into a class table and CSV, plus a Markdown rubric. Limitations: the GPU is a teaching model with invented costs and no caches, latency hiding or 2D indices, so cycle counts compare a student's own versions rather than predict hardware; blocks run in a fixed order, so the race detector stands in for real nondeterminism; values are untyped, so / truncates whenever both operands are whole; exports are unsigned files. 36 vitest tests, 99.2% statement coverage on core.
projects.publicNotes: Teaches parallel programming through twelve puzzle levels on a simulated graphics processor. Students write short programs in a simple language modeled on CUDA, pick how many threads to launch, and see exactly how groups of 32 threads run, where they slow down and where they collide. Levels cover indexing, branching, memory access patterns, data races and shared memory, with stars against a reference answer and hints that point at the line causing trouble. Instructors load students' progress files into a class table. Limitation: costs come from a teaching model, so they compare a student's own versions rather than predict real hardware speed.

projects.notes: Built in one session as a static site with no backend and no LLM. Students paste a JavaScript sample(rng, ...args); exact mode enumerates every draw sequence from a 1-16 bit source odometer-style and reports each outcome's probability as a BigInt fraction (rng.next() % 6 on 8 bits gives 43/256 vs 42/256), with rejection loops cut at 2^-32 and judged given termination; statistical mode runs a chi-square test on a seeded 32-bit xoshiro128** stream. Seven-bug gallery with fixes, shuffle position heat map, permalinks, and instructor exercise links (encoded in the URL) graded exact-first with a chi-square fallback at a stated false-fail rate. The suggested Pyodide/Python mode was left out; exact mode is exponential in draws, so large shuffles fall back to statistics. 68 vitest tests.
projects.publicNotes: Shows students exactly how a common random-number shortcut quietly favors some results. Paste a small JavaScript function that turns random bits into, say, a dice roll or a card shuffle, and it works out the exact chance of every outcome (43 in 256 versus 42 in 256 for a popular dice trick), or runs a statistical test when exact counting would take too long. A gallery of seven classic bugs with fixes and a shuffle heat map are built in, and instructors can share auto-graded exercises as links. Limitation: it only reads JavaScript, and large shuffles get a statistical test instead of exact answers.

projects.notes: Built in one session as a fully client-side tool for small WooCommerce/WordPress shops: the owner records two Chrome visits as HAR files (banner left alone, and after Reject all) and drops them in. It flags cookies and requests from about 25 advertising, analytics and embed services that fired before consent or after the rejection, splits the recording at the click by reading the banner's own consent cookie (Complianz, CookieYes, Cookiebot, OneTrust, Borlabs, Real Cookie Banner), and treats Google Consent Mode hits sent with consent denied as notes, not leaks. Each leak is traced to a plugin by following Chrome's _initiator chain to a /wp-content/plugins/<slug>/ file or by the WordPress handle id of the inline snippet, and it says plainly when a speed plugin (WP Rocket, Autoptimize, LiteSpeed...) or a PHP-set cookie hides the source. A saved check can be compared with a later one, naming the plugin that changed version behind a new leak. The idea's hosted headless-Chromium scanner with weekly rescans and email diffs was replaced by this do-it-yourself core, so nothing is uploaded and nothing runs on a schedule. 44 vitest tests, 100% statement coverage. Deployed via the GitHub Actions deploy workflow on netlify.app until the pisan.me CNAME exists.
projects.publicNotes: Checks whether your shop's cookie banner really blocks tracking until a visitor agrees. Record two visits in Chrome (one ignoring the banner, one clicking "Reject all") and drop the files in. It lists every advertising or analytics cookie that fired when it shouldn't have, and names the WordPress plugin responsible where it can. Nothing leaves your computer. Limitation: you run the check yourself; it doesn't watch the site automatically.

projects.notes: Fully client-side tool for small software vendors (edtech especially) asked for a VPAT before a university buys. The vendor describes the product, answers 12 yes/no product questions that settle Not Applicable criteria, and attaches axe-core 4.11.0 results per screen: a DevTools console snippet (loads axe from cdnjs, falls back to jsDelivr, copies results), an @axe-core/cli JSON file (one screen per page), or pasted page HTML that is stripped of scripts/handlers/javascript: links and scanned in a sandboxed iframe with the bundled axe-core. A guided review covers all 50 WCAG 2.1 A/AA criteria with plain-language tests, scan findings and outcome + evidence note. Fixed rules set level, remark and warnings: never Supports from a scan alone (clean + untested = Not Evaluated), a pass contradicted by scan failures becomes Partially Supports, every claim needs a note, Not Evaluated (not allowed for A/AA in VPAT 2.5) stamps the report DRAFT, 4.1.1 is Supports per the 2023 errata. Exports the VPAT 2.5 WCAG edition layout to Word (docx, lazy-loaded), HTML or print-to-PDF with screens-tested and evidence appendices; saved project files compare release to release. The idea's Playwright crawler, Supabase and Claude-drafted remarks were replaced by this browser-only, rule-based core. 48 vitest tests, 99% statement coverage; the app itself has zero axe WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light and dark mode. Deployed via the deploy workflow; the runner created the acr-draft.pisan.me CNAME.
projects.publicNotes: Helps small software companies write the accessibility report (a VPAT) that universities and public agencies ask for before they buy. You scan your key screens with a free checker, answer a short guided test for each accessibility rule, and download a finished report in Word, with the evidence behind every answer. It won't let you overstate your product: anything you haven't actually tested stays marked as a draft. Limitation: it can't do the hands-on testing for you, so the report is only as good as the checks you really carry out.

projects.notes: Vite + TypeScript page plus one stateless Netlify function (POST /api/step, GET /api/health). A test student walks eight Tutor LMS steps: home (critical error, maintenance, DB error, PHP warnings, Cloudflare challenge), login via /wp-login.php or a custom page (wrong password, CAPTCHA, 2FA and silent failure told apart, hidden fields kept), dashboard (login bounce, popup already open, course listed), course (enrolled vs Enroll Now, first lesson link), lesson (no-access text, YouTube no-referrer Error 153, empty players), quiz (opened, never started), certificate (Nonce not matched) and price as a logged-out visitor (struck-through sale prices, several currency formats). The browser calls the function once per step and carries the session cookies, so each call fits Netlify's 10 s limit (8.5 s network budget per step); the password goes only to the login step and nothing is stored. Requests are locked to the host typed in, each hop is DNS-checked against private/reserved ranges and non-web ports, redirects followed by hand. The same step code runs in the browser against a built-in demo academy with seven breakages from Aug-Oct 2026 Tutor support threads. The idea's Playwright worker, screenshots, Supabase schedules and daily email were replaced by on-demand HTML reading; alert email is generated as text to copy. No AI or paid API. 141 vitest tests, 99% statement coverage. First deploy's function crashed (esbuild ESM banner used import.meta, which Netlify's CJS re-bundle leaves undefined); fixed in 766d713 and redeployed, /api/health OK.
projects.publicNotes: Pretends to be one of your students and walks through your Tutor LMS course site the way they do: logging in, opening the dashboard, a course, a lesson and its video, a quiz, a certificate, and the price a new customer sees. Each step comes back as working, worth a look, or broken, in plain words with what to try next and an alert you can forward to whoever looks after your site. It is for coaches, tutors and small academies who sell courses from their own WordPress site, to run right after a plugin update. Limitation: it reads pages the way your server sends them and runs when you press the button, so problems that only appear when a script runs or a video actually plays can be missed, and there is no daily automatic check yet.

projects.notes: Fully client-side Vite + TypeScript app for faculty writing the teaching reflection in a promotion or tenure dossier. Comments come in as CSV exports (comment, course, term and question columns guessed; several comment columns per file kept with their question; N/A answers skipped) or pasted text per course and term; term labels in common forms (Fall 2024, SP25, 2024-25 Semester 2) are put in calendar order. Comments are split into clauses and sorted into 13 built-in themes plus user keyword themes; tone is a word list with negation, intensifiers, 'too <word>', contrast clauses and a sentence-level fallback, so one comment can be positive on clarity and critical on exams. A theme-by-term table per course; recorded course changes (user's own words, first term, linked themes auto-ticked) get before/after mention share and critical share, with 'too few to tell' under 5 mentions a side. Quote picker balances praise and criticism, spreads across terms, drops near-duplicates, honours pins/exclusions, and redacts titled names, listed names and emails. The reflection draft (intro, one paragraph per change with numbers and verbatim excerpts, strengths, still working on, bracketed placeholders) fits pages x words-per-page by trimming in a fixed order and says what it dropped; exports to Word (docx, lazy-loaded), text and a coded-comments CSV; projects save as local JSON, nothing uploaded. The idea's Claude clustering/drafting, Supabase and Stripe were replaced by this deterministic core. Built-in sample: about 230 generated comments, two courses, six semesters, two changes. 101 vitest tests, 99.5% statement coverage; zero axe WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light and dark mode. projects.publicNotes: Helps faculty going up for promotion or tenure write the reflection on student feedback that dossiers now ask for. You bring in years of course-evaluation comments, and it sorts them into themes, shows how comments changed after the course changes you made, picks a fair mix of praising and critical quotes with names removed, and drafts a reflection that fits your page limit, ready to edit in Word. Your comments never leave your browser. Limitation: it reads comments with word lists, so sarcasm and unusual phrasing can be misread, and a before-and-after difference is a count, not proof your change caused it.
